intro.en: Comprehensive clinical and surgical staging classifications defined by the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics for gynaecological cancers and gestational trophoblastic disease.

title.en: FIGO staging of carcinoma of the cervix

items.summary: Anatomical staging framework revised in 2018 permitting clinical, radiological, and pathological evaluation of tumour volume, local infiltration, and regional lymph node involvement.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Invasive carcinoma strictly confined to the cervix uteri (extension to the uterine corpus is disregarded).
Invasive carcinoma diagnosed exclusively by microscopy, with a maximum depth of stromal invasion < 5 mm.
Measured stromal invasion < 3 mm in maximum depth.
Measured stromal invasion >= 3 mm and < 5 mm in maximum depth.
Clinically visible lesion or microscopic lesion with depth of stromal invasion >= 5 mm.
Invasive carcinoma with stromal invasion >= 5 mm and greatest dimension < 2 cm.
Invasive carcinoma >= 2 cm and < 4 cm in maximum dimension.
Invasive carcinoma >= 4 cm in maximum dimension.
Carcinoma invades beyond the uterus but has not extended to the lower third of the vagina or to the pelvic side wall.
Involvement limited to the upper two-thirds of the vagina without parametrial infiltration.
Invasive carcinoma < 4 cm in maximum dimension.
Invasive carcinoma >= 4 cm in maximum dimension.
Parametrial infiltration present but not extending onto the pelvic wall.
Tumour extends to the pelvic wall, involves the lower third of the vagina, causes hydronephrosis or non-functioning kidney, or involves regional lymph nodes.
Carcinoma involves the lower third of the vagina with no extension onto the pelvic wall.
Tumour extends onto the pelvic wall, or causes hydronephrosis or a non-functioning kidney (unless attributable to other causes).
Metastasis to regional pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes confirmed by imaging or pathology, irrespective of primary tumour dimensions.
Carcinoma extending beyond the true pelvis or biopsy-proven infiltration of bladder or rectal mucosa.
Spread of malignancy to adjacent pelvic mucosal organs (bladder or rectum).
Distant metastatic dissemination to extrapelvic organs.

blocks.title: Key staging principles and practical notes
bullets: FIGO 2018 incorporated cross-sectional imaging and pathology into cervical cancer staging, moving beyond purely clinical assessment.
Horizontal linear spread is no longer used to separate IA1 from IA2; only measured stromal depth of invasion (< 3 mm vs 3 to < 5 mm) applies.
Lymph node involvement is designated with an r suffix for radiological detection or p suffix for histological confirmation (e.g. IIIC1p).
Hydronephrosis automatically upstages a lesion to IIIB even if physical parametrial spread does not reach the pelvic wall.

viva.q: What major modification did the 2018 FIGO cervical cancer staging introduce regarding lymph node involvement?
viva.a: Stage IIIC was created to classify regional lymph node involvement, split into IIIC1 for pelvic nodes and IIIC2 for para-aortic nodal metastases verified by imaging or pathology.

viva.q: How is microscopic stage IA cervical cancer differentiated from clinically evident stage IB?
viva.a: Stage IA comprises microscopic lesions invading < 5 mm into stroma; stage IB includes lesions invading >= 5 mm or any macroscopic clinically visible tumour.

viva.q: Which findings assign a patient to stage IIIB in cervical cancer?
viva.a: Extension of tumour to the pelvic sidewall, or hydronephrosis and non-functioning kidney proven secondary to malignant ureteric obstruction.

title.en: FIGO staging of carcinoma of the endometrium

items.summary: Surgical and pathological staging system for endometrial carcinoma based on depth of myometrial infiltration, cervical stromal spread, local extension, and nodal status.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Tumour strictly confined to the uterine corpus.
No myometrial invasion or invasion limited to less than half of the myometrial thickness.
Tumour invasion equal to or exceeding half of the myometrial thickness.
Tumour invades the cervical stroma but remains confined within the uterus.
Local or regional tumour dissemination beyond the uterine body.
Tumour invades the uterine serosa and/or adnexal structures (fallopian tubes or ovaries).
Metastatic involvement of regional pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes.
Positive para-aortic lymph nodes with or without positive pelvic lymph nodes.
Tumour invades bladder or bowel mucosa, or distant metastatic dissemination.
Tumour invasion into the mucosal lining of the urinary bladder or bowel.
Distant metastases, including intra-abdominal peritoneal spread, liver, lungs, or inguinal lymph nodes.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: Endometrial cancer staging is primarily surgical, requiring total hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and appropriate nodal assessment.
Endocervical glandular involvement alone is classified as stage I; stromal invasion of the cervix is mandatory for stage II designation.
Positive peritoneal cytology alone without peritoneal lesions does not alter the official FIGO surgical stage but should be recorded separately.

viva.q: How does depth of myometrial invasion determine stage I endometrial carcinoma?
viva.a: Stage IA denotes tumour limited to the endometrium or invading < half the myometrium, whereas stage IB indicates myometrial invasion >= half the wall thickness.

viva.q: What distinguishes stage II from stage III endometrial carcinoma?
viva.a: Stage II involves cervical stromal infiltration without extrauterine spread, while stage III exhibits local or regional extension beyond the uterus to adnexa, vagina, or lymph nodes.

viva.q: How is regional nodal involvement categorized in endometrial cancer staging?
viva.a: Stage IIIC is divided into IIIC1 for regional pelvic lymph node metastases and IIIC2 for positive para-aortic lymph nodes with or without pelvic involvement.

unsure: Source text lists distant metastases (liver, lungs, inguinal lymph nodes) under a duplicate heading of Stage IVA instead of Stage IVB; standard FIGO assigns distant spread to Stage IVB.

title.en: FIGO staging of ovarian, fallopian tube, and peritoneal cancer

aka: Ovary and fallopian tube cancer staging
items.summary: Unified surgical and pathological staging framework for epithelial carcinomas of the ovary, fallopian tube, and peritoneum based on capsular breach, pelvic spread, and peritoneal implants.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Tumour strictly confined to the ovaries or fallopian tubes.
Tumour limited to one ovary or fallopian tube; capsule intact; no tumour on ovarian surface; negative peritoneal washings or ascites.
Tumour involves both ovaries or fallopian tubes; capsules intact; no surface tumour; negative peritoneal washings or ascites.
Tumour limited to one or both ovaries or fallopian tubes with intraoperative spill, capsular rupture, surface growth, or malignant ascites/washings.
Iatrogenic intraoperative surgical capsule rupture and spill.
Capsule ruptured prior to surgery or tumour present on ovarian or fallopian tube surface.
Malignant cells demonstrated in ascites or peritoneal washings.
Tumour involves one or both ovaries or fallopian tubes with pelvic extension below the pelvic brim, or primary peritoneal malignancy.
Tumour extension or implants on the uterus, fallopian tubes, or ovaries.
Tumour extension to other pelvic intraperitoneal tissues.
Tumour involves one or both ovaries or fallopian tubes with cytologically or histologically confirmed peritoneal metastases beyond the pelvis and/or retroperitoneal lymph node metastases.
Positive retroperitoneal lymph nodes only (proven histologically or cytologically).
Retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis <= 10 mm in greatest dimension.
Retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis > 10 mm in greatest dimension.
Microscopic extrapelvic peritoneal involvement with or without positive retroperitoneal lymph nodes.
Macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal metastasis <= 2 cm in greatest dimension; retroperitoneal nodes may or may not be positive; liver/spleen capsule may be involved.
Macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal metastasis > 2 cm in greatest dimension; retroperitoneal nodes may or may not be positive; liver/spleen capsule may be involved without parenchymal spread.
Distant metastatic dissemination excluding peritoneal metastases.
Pleural effusion demonstrating positive malignant cytology.
Parenchymal metastases to the liver or spleen; extra-abdominal organ metastases; inguinal or other lymph nodes outside the abdominal cavity.

blocks.title: Key staging criteria
bullets: Surgical staging entails meticulous peritoneal inspection, bilateral pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy, infracolic omentectomy, and peritoneal washings.
Capsule rupture is differentiated: IC1 for intraoperative surgical spill versus IC2 for spontaneous preoperative capsular breach.
Hepatic or splenic surface capsular implants are classified as stage III; true parenchymal infiltration is required for stage IVB designation.

viva.q: How does capsular status affect stage I ovarian carcinoma classification?
viva.a: Intact capsules denote IA (single ovary) or IB (bilateral); capsular spill or surface growth upstages the disease to IC (IC1 for surgical rupture, IC2 for preoperative breach, IC3 for positive washings).

viva.q: What criteria differentiate stage IIIA, IIIB, and IIIC in ovarian cancer?
viva.a: Stage IIIA represents retroperitoneal nodal involvement or microscopic peritoneal spread; IIIB denotes macroscopic peritoneal implants <= 2 cm; IIIC denotes peritoneal deposits > 2 cm.

viva.q: When is pleural effusion classified as stage IVA in ovarian cancer?
viva.a: Pleural effusion constitutes stage IVA only when diagnostic thoracocentesis reveals positive malignant cytology; benign transudative effusion does not upstage disease.

title.en: FIGO staging of carcinoma of the vulva

items.summary: Surgical and pathological staging system for vulvar malignancy evaluating primary lesion size, depth of stromal invasion, adjacent organ spread, and inguinofemoral lymph node status.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Tumour confined to the vulva or perineum with negative regional lymph nodes.
Lesion <= 2 cm in greatest dimension with measured stromal invasion <= 1.0 mm, negative nodes.
Lesion > 2 cm in dimension or stromal invasion > 1.0 mm, negative nodes.
Tumour of any size with direct extension to adjacent perineal structures (lower third of urethra, lower third of vagina, anus) with negative nodes.
Tumour of any size with adjacent spread and/or positive inguinofemoral lymph nodes.
Regional lymph node metastasis: 1 node deposit >= 5 mm, or 1 to 2 node deposits < 5 mm.
Metastasis to 1 lymph node measuring >= 5 mm.
Metastasis to 1 or 2 lymph nodes measuring < 5 mm.
Regional lymph node metastasis: >= 2 node deposits >= 5 mm, or >= 3 node deposits < 5 mm.
Metastasis to 2 or more lymph nodes measuring >= 5 mm.
Metastasis to 3 or more lymph nodes measuring < 5 mm.
Positive regional lymph node or nodes exhibiting extracapsular tumour extension.
Tumour invades other regional structures or distant sites.
Tumour invades upper two-thirds of urethra, upper two-thirds of vagina, bladder/rectal mucosa, pelvic bone, or fixed/ulcerated inguinofemoral nodes.
Direct invasion into upper urethra, upper vagina, bladder mucosa, rectal mucosa, or fixed attachment to pelvic bone.
Fixed or ulcerated inguinofemoral lymph node metastases.
Any distant metastasis, including deep pelvic lymph node metastases.

blocks.title: Staging rules and prognostic factors
bullets: Depth of invasion is measured from the epithelial-stromal junction of the adjacent most superficial dermal papilla to the deepest point of malignant infiltration.
Inguinofemoral lymph node status constitutes the single most critical prognostic determinant in invasive vulvar carcinoma.
Deep pelvic lymph node involvement (iliac or obturator) signifies distant metastatic spread and is designated as stage IVB.

viva.q: What exact histological parameters distinguish stage IA from stage IB vulvar carcinoma?
viva.a: Stage IA requires tumour <= 2 cm and stromal invasion <= 1.0 mm with negative nodes; tumours > 2 cm or invasion > 1.0 mm are classified as stage IB.

viva.q: How does the number and size of involved lymph nodes determine stage III vulvar cancer?
viva.a: Stage IIIA has 1 node >= 5 mm or 1-2 nodes < 5 mm; IIIB has >= 2 nodes >= 5 mm or >= 3 nodes < 5 mm; IIIC has extracapsular spread.

viva.q: Which clinical presentations categorise vulvar cancer as stage IVA?
viva.a: Invasion of upper vagina, upper urethra, bladder or rectal mucosa, fixation to pelvic bone, or fixed or ulcerated inguinofemoral lymph nodes.

title.en: FIGO staging of carcinoma of the vagina

items.summary: Clinical and anatomical staging system for primary invasive carcinoma of the vagina evaluating vaginal confinement, paravaginal infiltration, pelvic sidewall extension, and distant metastases.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Carcinoma strictly confined to the vaginal wall.
Carcinoma involves paravaginal tissues but does not extend onto the pelvic side wall.
Carcinoma extends to the pelvic wall, involves the lower third of the vagina, causes hydronephrosis/non-functioning kidney, or involves pelvic or inguinal lymph nodes.
Carcinoma extends beyond the true pelvis or has involved the mucosa of the bladder or rectum (proven on biopsy).
Tumour invades bladder or rectal mucosa, or exhibits direct extension beyond the pelvic cavity; regional lymph nodes may or may not be positive.
Distant metastatic dissemination to distant organs or tissues.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: Primary vaginal carcinoma is uncommon; malignancy involving both cervix and vagina is categorized as cervical cancer, and vulvar involvement is staged as vulvar cancer.
Lymphatic drainage depends on anatomical location: upper two-thirds drain to pelvic lymph nodes, while the lower third drains to inguinofemoral nodes.
Stage III encompasses involvement of regional pelvic or inguinal lymph nodes or hydronephrosis secondary to lateral pelvic extension.

viva.q: What rule governs the diagnosis of primary vaginal carcinoma versus cervical or vulvar malignancy?
viva.a: Any malignant tumour involving both cervix and vagina is staged as cervical cancer, while any tumour involving both vulva and vagina is staged as vulvar cancer.

viva.q: Which findings place a vaginal carcinoma into stage III?
viva.a: Extension of disease to the pelvic sidewall, tumour reaching the lower third of the vagina, hydronephrosis, or regional pelvic or inguinal lymph node metastasis.

viva.q: What constitutes stage IVA in carcinoma of the vagina?
viva.a: Biopsy-proven invasion into the mucosal lining of the bladder or rectum, or direct extension of malignant tumour beyond the boundaries of the true pelvis.

aka: Leiomyosarcoma and endometrial stromal sarcoma staging
items.summary: Surgical and pathological staging classification for uterine leiomyosarcoma and endometrial stromal sarcoma based on uterine confinement, pelvic extension, extrapelvic abdominal disease, and distant spread.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Tumour strictly confined to the uterine body.
Tumour confined to the uterus measuring <= 5 cm in greatest dimension.
Tumour confined to the uterus measuring > 5 cm in greatest dimension.
Tumour extends beyond the uterus but remains confined within the pelvic cavity.
Tumour involves adnexal structures (ovaries or fallopian tubes).
Tumour extends to other extrauterine pelvic tissues.
Tumour invades abdominal tissues outside the pelvic cavity.
Tumour involves abdominal tissues at one site only.
Tumour involves abdominal tissues at more than one site.
Metastatic involvement of regional pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes.
Advanced tumour invasion into mucosal pelvic organs or distant organ metastasis.
Tumour invades the mucosal lining of the urinary bladder or rectum.

blocks.title: Clinical points to remember
bullets: This staging framework applies specifically to leiomyosarcomas, endometrial stromal sarcomas, and undifferentiated uterine sarcomas.
Uterine carcinosarcoma (malignant mixed Mullerian tumour) is an epithelial malignancy and must be staged according to endometrial adenocarcinoma criteria.
Haematogenous dissemination to the lungs and liver is more prevalent in uterine sarcomas than lymphatic spread.

viva.q: How is stage I uterine leiomyosarcoma subclassified by tumour dimensions?
viva.a: Stage IA denotes a tumour <= 5 cm in greatest dimension confined to the uterus, whereas stage IB denotes a uterine-confined tumour > 5 cm.

viva.q: What anatomical distinction separates stage IIA from stage IIB in uterine sarcoma?
viva.a: Stage IIA denotes extrauterine spread limited to the adnexa, while stage IIB denotes extension into other extrauterine pelvic soft tissues.

viva.q: How should uterine carcinosarcoma be staged?
viva.a: Carcinosarcomas are metaplastic carcinomas and must be staged according to the FIGO staging system for endometrial carcinoma, not uterine sarcoma.

unsure: Source text lists tumour size as '< 5 cm' for both Stage IA and Stage IB; standard FIGO defines Stage IA as <= 5 cm and Stage IB as > 5 cm. Left the ambiguous source duplicate out and noted here.

title.en: FIGO staging of adenosarcoma of the uterus

items.summary: Specialised surgical and pathological staging framework for uterine adenosarcomas graded by depth of myometrial invasion, pelvic extension, extrapelvic abdominal disease, and distant spread.

head: Stage
Anatomical extent and criteria
rows: Tumour strictly confined to the uterus.
Tumour limited to the endometrium or endocervix with no myometrial invasion.
Tumour invasion limited to less than or equal to half (<= 50%) of the myometrial thickness.
Tumour invasion extending to greater than half (> 50%) of the myometrial thickness.
Tumour extends beyond the uterus into the pelvic cavity.
Tumour involves adnexal structures (ovaries or fallopian tubes).
Tumour extends to other extrauterine pelvic tissues.
Tumour invades abdominal tissues beyond the pelvis (not merely protruding into the abdomen).
Tumour invades abdominal tissues at a single site.
Tumour invades abdominal tissues at more than one site.
Metastatic involvement of regional pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes.
Advanced tumour invasion into pelvic mucosal organs or distant metastases.
Direct mucosal invasion into the urinary bladder or rectum.
Distant organ metastases (such as liver or lungs).

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Adenosarcomas are mixed biphasic tumours with benign glandular epithelium and a malignant mesenchymal stroma.
Depth of myometrial invasion (none in IA, <= half in IB, > half in IC) is the most critical pathological prognostic factor for uterine-confined disease.
Sarcomatous overgrowth (defined as sarcomatous element occupying >= 25% of the tumour volume) conveys a substantially higher risk of recurrence and metastasis.

viva.q: How is stage I uterine adenosarcoma subclassified based on myometrial invasion?
viva.a: Stage IA has no myometrial invasion; stage IB invades <= half the myometrium; stage IC invades > half the myometrial thickness.

viva.q: What distinguishes stage IIIA from stage IIIB adenosarcoma?
viva.a: Stage IIIA involves extrapelvic abdominal tissues at one site only, whereas stage IIIB denotes tumour spread to more than one abdominal site.

viva.q: What is sarcomatous overgrowth in adenosarcoma and why is it clinically important?
viva.a: It is defined by pure high-grade sarcoma occupying >= 25% of the tumour; it markedly increases the risk of deep myometrial invasion, nodal spread, and distant recurrence.

title.en: FIGO staging and prognostic scoring for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

aka: Gestational trophoblastic disease WHO FIGO prognostic score
items.summary: Dual classification combining anatomical tumour staging with the WHO/FIGO modified prognostic risk score to guide single-agent versus multi-agent chemotherapy regimens.

head: Stage
Anatomical disease extent
rows: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia strictly confined to the uterine corpus.
Gestational trophoblastic disease extends outside the uterus but is limited to genital structures (fallopian tubes, ovaries, vagina, broad ligament).
Gestational trophoblastic disease extends to the lungs, with or without genital tract involvement.
Gestational trophoblastic disease involves other distant metastatic sites (e.g. liver, spleen, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, brain).

blocks.title: Risk stratification and clinical implications
bullets: Low-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: total FIGO prognostic score of 0 to 6; managed primarily with single-agent chemotherapy (intramuscular methotrexate or intravenous actinomycin D).
High-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: total FIGO prognostic score >= 7 (or any stage IV disease); requires multi-agent chemotherapy, typically the EMA-CO regimen.

High-risk GTN has significant potential for chemo-resistance and intracranial haemorrhage; brain metastases mandate urgent whole-brain radiotherapy or stereotactic treatment with intrathecal methotrexate.

viva.q: How is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia stratified into low-risk and high-risk categories?
viva.a: Using the FIGO/WHO prognostic scoring system: a score of 0 to 6 indicates low-risk disease, whereas a score >= 7 designates high-risk disease requiring multi-agent chemotherapy.

viva.q: What constitutes stage III in the anatomical staging of GTN?
viva.a: Stage III indicates pulmonary metastases demonstrated on chest radiography or CT, with or without concurrent genital tract involvement.

viva.q: Which metastatic sites carry the highest prognostic score in the FIGO scoring system?
viva.a: Brain and liver metastases carry a score of 4 each due to high risks of haemorrhage, chemo-resistance, and mortality.

unsure: Source text lists WHO/FIGO scores with column headings '0, 1, 2, 3' for chemotherapy and intervals, whereas classic scoring assigns 4 to the highest tier; preserved exact categories from source table.
